claims.text: Light cold rolling of the FeNiCrCoCu coating increases its initial dislocation density relative to the as-deposited state.
A higher initial dislocation density lowers the nucleation or energy barrier for stress-induced epsilon-martensite formation.
FeNiCrCoCu undergoes a stress-induced, diffusionless transformation to epsilon martensite during high-temperature sliding.
The c/a ratio of epsilon martensite in transformative HEAs can evolve with processing and deformation.
The transformation during sliding lowers the intrinsic c/a ratio of the epsilon phase in FeNiCrCoCu.
A lower-than-ideal epsilon-phase c/a ratio promotes non-basal pyramidal 〈c+a〉 slip and deformation twinning.
Non-basal 〈c+a〉 slip and deformation twinning improve accommodation of strain along the h.c.p. c-axis.
The additional slip and twinning modes mitigate localized stress concentrations and localized damage.
Mitigation of localized damage by these deformation modes reduces wear and friction.
At approximately 600°C, thermal activation promotes the proposed stress-induced phase transformation.
After sliding at approximately 600°C, the pre-deformed coating will contain a statistically higher epsilon-martensite fraction than the as-deposited coating.
After sliding, the pre-deformed coating will have a higher twin-boundary density than the as-deposited coating.
The pre-deformed coating will exhibit a lower friction coefficient than the as-deposited coating.
The pre-deformed coating will exhibit a lower wear rate than the as-deposited coating.
Temperatures outside the approximately 600°C regime may alter transformation kinetics.
Thermal recovery at or near 600°C may erase the pre-induced dislocation structure and diminish the proposed wear benefit.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant increase in epsilon martensite and twin boundaries, or failure to improve wear and friction, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
